source.title: Emergent Hierarchical Monosemantic Neurons from the Group-Contrastive Forward-Forward Algorithm
source.authors: Yi-Ming Tang; Qinglin Qi; Zhao-Qian Yao; Harshvardhan Saini; Dian-Bo Liu

record.tranche_reason: The study proposes and evaluates GCFF as a method for producing interpretable, monosemantic features. Its neurons are deliberately trained with class-specific routing and contrastive objectives, so their measured coherence does not test whether polysemanticity occurs without that inducement.
record.gate_note: The paper reports LLM alignment scores for 430 GCFF-selected neurons and qualitative feature examples. These are results about neurons produced by the study's purpose-built method, not a measurement of naturally occurring polysemanticity. The classification benchmarks evaluate a separate use of GCFF and do not measure the claim. Cited findings are not recorded as rows.
record.test_reason: The study builds a purpose-made interpretation module (GCFF) with class-specific routing and contrastive objectives meant to yield monosemantic neurons, then scores only its own top-selected neurons. It never measures how often polysemanticity arises in naturally trained networks, its cause, or its dependence on architecture or measurement. Polysemanticity due to superposition is cited from prior work only.
record.authors_conclusion: Correct: a GCFF module on CLIP representations yields monosemantic neurons whose abstraction increases with depth, without sparsity or abstraction supervision. The authors also claim GCFF is state of the art among forward-forward classifiers.
record.recipe_differences: The study trains a class-routed, contrastive forward-forward interpretation module; it does not reproduce the original neuron identification or intervention method.

fits_no_version.finding: GCFF neurons pre-selected by internal consistency (top 20 per layer) got mean LLM alignment scores of 0.829 and 0.824 from two evaluators.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: A class-routed forward-forward module trained on CLIP embeddings yields selected neurons that LLM evaluators rate as semantically consistent, with qualitatively increasing abstraction across depth.

record.problems: The coherence evaluation uses LLM-generated captions and explanations, and evaluates only the top 20 neurons per layer selected using an internal-consistency screen. No control or comparison of naturally occurring neurons is reported, and no uncertainty estimates are given for the alignment scores.
record.rows_left_out: The paper reports evaluator agreement (91.0%) and Cohen’s κ (0.687) in Table 1, but these assess agreement between evaluators rather than neuron polysemanticity. Qualitative examples and hierarchy descriptions are also not recorded as polysemanticity measurements.

untested.parts: No measurement of neurons in image classifiers such as InceptionV1 responding to unrelated inputs.
Superposition is cited (Elhage et al. 2022) as the cause but not tested.
No test of polysemanticity arising without capacity pressure.

Polysemantic shares are not compared across activations or architectures of naturally trained models. GCFF classification accuracy (Table 2) is not paired with any polysemanticity rate in those networks.
Canonical polysemantic neurons are not re-examined.
Activation ranges and scoring methods are not compared. Only top-20 images are scored, using one LLM pipeline.

record.verdict_notes: Some GCFF neurons in the qualitative figures are themselves mixtures (e.g. Layer 2 Neuron 75 'chain, knot, padlock, necklace, and hook'; Layer 3 Neuron 5). The authors frame these as functional groupings. This is anecdotal, concerns the study's own module, and is not counted as evidence for V6.

versions.untested_parts: The study does not test mixed responses in neurons of image classifiers such as InceptionV1.
No transformer language model neurons or language-model token/context responses are tested.
The study does not test whether polysemanticity is caused by superposition or capacity pressure.
The study does not test whether polysemanticity arises from initialization, regularization, or training noise when capacity is sufficient.

GCFF is designed to produce coherent features, but the paper does not compare naturally occurring polysemantic-neuron shares across architectures or training conditions, nor show that such a share is lowered without a large performance loss.
The study does not re-examine canonical polysemantic neurons or establish that their mixed inputs share a feature.
The study does not compare polysemanticity judgments across activation ranges or explanation-scoring methods as a test of this version.

rows.note: Aggregate result across the selected neurons; the paper describes the learned neurons as highly explainable and selective. This evaluates intentionally trained GCFF neurons, not naturally occurring polysemanticity.
